name: Duration with for
pattern: clause with adjunct PP[for + measure NP of time]

entry.name: Duration with for
entry.pattern: clause with adjunct PP[for + measure NP of time]

1.definition: Measures how long a state, process or maintained result holds.

relatedConstructions.notes: Wrote for an hour measures time spent writing. Wrote the letter in an hour measures elapsed time to completion.

projection.target: The adjunct measures holding time. With a normally punctual predicate it can favour a repeated-event or resulting-state construal where supported by context.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Saying how long with for
curious.summary: A for phrase with a length of time says how long something lasted.
curious.body: In Jo stayed outside for fifteen minutes, for fifteen minutes measures how long Jo's staying outside lasted. It can measure how long a state or an activity held, or a result was maintained. Compare time measured by in. Wrote for an hour measures the time spent writing, while wrote the letter in an hour measures the time it took to finish. With a very quick action, the for phrase can suggest repetition or a result that lasts, where the context supports that.

examples.text: Jo wrote the letter [in an hour].

curious.try: Say how long you spent on something today, using for. Then say how long a finished job took, using in.

teacher.summary: Helps explain for-phrases that measure how long, and how they differ from in-phrases that measure time to completion.
teacher.explain: A for-PP with a measure NP of time is an adjunct that measures how long a state, process or maintained result holds: Jo stayed outside for fifteen minutes. Wrote for an hour measures time spent writing, while wrote the letter in an hour measures elapsed time to completion. With a normally punctual predicate, the adjunct can favour a repeated-event or resulting-state construal where context supports it. This dictionary treats it as a specialization of the PP and marks it provisional, with medium confidence.
teacher.terms: For-phrases like this are sometimes called duration adverbials.

contrasts.text: Jo wrote the letter in an hour.

watch_for: A learner might mix up for an hour (time spent) and in an hour (time to finish).
A learner might read for fifteen minutes with a quick action as one long event, when context can favour a repeated-event reading.
teacher.activity: Give students a list of activities, some open-ended (reading, waiting) and some with an endpoint (writing a letter, cleaning a room). They add for or in plus a time and explain what each phrase measures.

child.hook: How do you say how long Jo stayed outside?
child.explain: For and a length of time tell how long something lasted. Jo stayed outside for fifteen minutes. The time is how long she stayed.
child.play: Tell a partner something you did today. Say how long it lasted using for. Your partner guesses what you did.
